title_en: How Do You Know the Last Case Was the Last?
title_zh: 没有发现病例，怎样知道真的没有了？
deck_en: The work did not end when reports reached zero. Surveillance, changing methods and international certification made absence credible—without settling every question about how people were treated.
deck_zh: 报表上的零，不是工作的终点。从查找疑似病例、调整接种办法到国际认证，读人怎样有根据地相信疾病已经消失，又不让成果替所有现场手段作答。

body_zh: 一项要宣布成功的计划，最后还认真保存了一本“传闻登记簿”。里面不是值得庆祝的数字，而是可能把庆祝打断的消息：某处是不是又出现了天花？有一个疑似病例，要不要去查？
世界卫生组织从1978年1月建立国际天花传闻登记。全球认证委员会的报告记载，到1979年底，四十个被认为已无天花的国家直接向WHO报告了一百零四条传闻。那不是全世界所有地方报告的总数，也不是一百零四个确诊病例。[1]
一本为成功保存坏消息入口的簿子，有点不合我们的习惯。越接近完成，我们往往越希望新来的问题别再打乱结论。但这里的工作恰恰要求相反：如果真要说疾病消失了，就得让可能证明它没消失的消息进得来。
## 零也可能是没有找到
1967年，全球强化消灭天花计划开始运行。它后来取得了真实而重大的成果：最后一个已知自然发生病例于1977年出现在索马里，1980年WHO宣告天花根除。可若从结果往前看，路上每一步都容易显得像早已知道终点。[5]
当年的工作人员并没有这种方便。他们要区分两种表面相同的报表：一张写零，是因为真的没有病例；另一张也写零，却可能因为病人没有进入卫生系统，消息没能送到，或原有的查找办法根本看不到那里。数字相同，事情完全不同。
接种人数也不能代替这个分别。做了多少次接种，回答的是完成了多少工作；传播链是否仍在，问的是疾病在哪里继续。前一个数字很重要，但不能因为它便于加总，就让后一个问题消失。
计划的负责人之一亨德森在1980年的回顾里说，1967年的操作手册已经把监测列为核心：收集资料、分析、采取行动、把结果送回有关人员。它不是后来才突然想到要记录病例，而是要让一开始写进办法里的东西，真正改变现场工作。[2]
这点尤其值得留意。一份手册早有正确的话，不意味着组织实际把同样多的时间和注意力给了它。一个人可以赞成需要调查，同时继续按最熟悉、最容易报成绩的办法忙到没有时间调查。办法写在那里，与办法能够纠正我们，是两回事。
亨德森提到尼日利亚东部的经验：有针对性的疫情围堵接种与报告，可以在并未达到很高整体免疫覆盖的地方切断传播；类似经验后来得到其他地区印证。把注意力转向传播发生在哪里，给行动带来了另一种可能。[2]
这不是“疫苗没有用，所以改做调查”。恰好相反，有效疫苗仍是重要工具；改变的是工具怎样跟着证据使用。发现病例、找接触者、及时组织接种与处置，把原本只是总量的工作，转向具体仍在发生的传播。
也不要把转向写成一纸新命令立即替换旧办法。亨德森的叙述承认，许多国家负责人和顾问熟悉并相信大规模接种，让监测获得足够重视，比看到它的意义困难得多。现场认识可以走在组织习惯前面，旧办法却未必因此立刻让路。[2]
印度的历史研究又把这个过程拆得更细。桑乔伊·巴塔查里亚依据档案指出，WHO总部、区域人员、印度中央与地方机关之间有持续交涉和摩擦；改变既需要资源，也需要反复取得支持。把它说成国际专家带来正确方案、地方只负责执行，会把真正做成这件事的人和工作一起删掉。[3]
所以，全球合作的能力不只在远处。总部可以协调资源和技术，具体病例却要由当地的人发现，消息要被送出，还得有人赶得过去。没有这些连接，一个世界性的目标也可能只是许多地方同时收不到回音。
## 最后一个病例之后，还要继续找
我们现在知道1977年的索马里病例是最后一个自然病例；当时却不能因为已经出现一个“最后”，就把这个称呼直接交给它。认证所要确认的，正是后来没有另一例被漏掉。这个问题不能靠给前一例起名字来解决。
国际认证把经过的时间与查找能力放在一起：距最后病例至少两年，并有足以发现病例的监测。不是把日历翻满两年，便自动换来一张合格证。若找不到的原因还不清楚，等待本身不会使那个零更可靠。[1]
可以把这个分别放在身边理解。你说一件东西不在房间里，别人会问你看过哪里、有没有开灯、柜子里是否也找了。不是要求你永远不能下结论，而是问这次没看见，究竟有多少理由被当作不存在。认证把类似的认真放到了更大的事情里。
传闻登记的意义也在这里。报告中的条目包含后来被辨认为其他疾病或旧病例的消息；其中两例确诊天花来自1978年伯明翰的实验室相关暴发。因此，“最后一个自然病例”绝不能偷换成“此后再没发生过任何天花病例”。[1]
把一条疑似消息核实为别的疾病，不是白跑一趟。它既没有为了维持成功而把消息压下去，也没有只因听到消息便宣布整个判断失效。发现、检查和给出结论，是三步；认真接纳第一步，不等于跳过后两步。
这也解释了为什么核查仍然需要判断。一个系统若把所有疑似都永远算成确诊，就永远不能完成工作；若只接收能维持零的材料，又根本不配相信那个零。它得有办法让消息进来，再用可说明的方法把它查清楚。
国际委员会所做的，不是只替国家的宣布再盖一枚更大的章。材料审查与现场核查要给出足够理由；全球委员会再汇集这些证据。WHO报告的序言记录，1980年5月8日，世界卫生大会接受了委员会的根除结论。[1]
这份结论当然很有分量。但它之所以值得信任，不只是因为说话的人位置高，更因为在结论前面有一段允许被追问的工作：为什么没有发现，怎样判断不是漏掉，另一个地方提供的材料能不能同样被检查。
跨国合作在这里创造了很具体的东西：人不必只凭另一个国家说“我们好了”便相信，也不必因永远无法亲自遍查世界而什么都不信。共同组织查找、检验与认证，给彼此的信任提供了可用的根据。
但方法能够学习，不是说所有问题都只剩技术调整。病例能被看见以后，还有一个问题会走进来：为了尽快把数字归零，工作人员可以怎样对待眼前这个人？
## 成果不能替每一种手段作答
历史学者保罗·格里诺的研究，回顾了1973至1975年南亚消灭天花工作的若干威吓和强制事件，并讨论由此引起的抵触。这些是需要认真面对的具体记录；它们不能被扩大成所有地区、所有工作人员的共同做法，也不能仅凭个案算出整个计划的发生比例。[4]
这里不必在两个极端里挑一个。天花消灭了，不表示每一次进入家庭、施压和接种都得到认可；存在不当手段，也不表示疫苗、查找和国际协作没有真实地保护生命。前一项成果不能替后一项疑问回答，后一项疑问也不要求我们否认前一项。
处在传播风险里的人，与要对其采取行动的人，都有不能只用一句话打发的理由。健康风险不会因拒绝便只落在拒绝者自己身上；保护别人的需要，也不能免去说明干预依据、范围与具体做法的责任。困难就在两边都不能被轻轻擦掉。
一国参加共同计划，与某个人愿意接受一次现场行动，仍然不是同一份同意。我们不能用国家间的合作文件替个人补一声赞成，也不能只看到国际目标，就认定地方的犹疑只能来自无知。要判断一个冲突，还需知道那一处究竟发生了什么。
散文的空间，正好应该留给这样的分辨。不是为一个成功事迹挑几条缺点，以显示态度平衡；而是把不同问题放回各自位置：疾病是否被消灭，怎样知道，谁做出了什么工作，以及某个人有没有受到不该忽略的对待。
根除后的安排也没有把查找与防范全部撤掉。WHO后来回顾，1980年的后续政策仍包括疑似病例调查、实验室病毒库存管理和保留必要能力。成功改变了接下来需要做什么，却没有让一切警惕从此多余。[6]
反过来，能够继续调查，也不意味着永远不得宣布一项真实成果。否则所有证据都只能变成“还不够”的理由，人也永远无法据此改变生活。值得追求的不是无限推迟结论，而是结论有根据，且不把以后相关的材料提前宣布为无关。
这篇的历史止于1980年的认证与后续安排。它不是把当年工具和干预办法直接推荐给今天，也不把一种疾病的经验当作所有疾病都可照搬的模板。我们在这里读的，是人怎样在不知道结局时，逐步形成足以采取行动和作出判断的根据。
回到那本登记簿，它最动人的地方也许不是条目后来没有推翻根除结论，而是一个接近成功的计划，仍为可能打断自己的人留了入口。真正有分量的“我们做到了”，不必靠从此不再听见疑问来维持。
body_en: Near the end of the smallpox eradication campaign, the work included keeping a register of rumours. This was not a collection of inspiring stories. It held reports that might interrupt the approaching celebration: someone, somewhere, might still have smallpox. A programme preparing to announce success had organized a route for unwelcome news.

WHO established its international rumour register in January 1978. The Global Commission’s report records 104 reports received directly from forty countries considered smallpox-free by the end of 1979. They were neither 104 confirmed cases nor a count of every local rumour in the world. They were matters to investigate.[1]

The distinction gives the register its interest. As a task approaches completion, questions can start to sound like obstruction. Here, confidence depended on keeping a way open for information that might show the task was not complete. The programme needed something more demanding than an absence of objections: it needed reasons to trust an absence of disease.
## Zero can mean that nobody found it

The intensified global programme began in 1967. Its achievement was substantial: the last known naturally occurring case was recorded in Somalia in 1977, and WHO declared eradication in 1980. Knowing the outcome, we can too easily make the intervening work look like a journey whose destination was already visible.[5]

Those doing the work had no such advantage. A report could contain zero because no cases existed. It could also contain zero because someone was outside the health system, information had not travelled, or the search did not reach the right place. The written result could be identical while the situations were entirely different.

A vaccination total could not settle that difference. It described work performed, not necessarily every remaining chain of transmission. Counting activity was useful. Substituting it for the question of where disease persisted would make the convenient number answer a different question from the one that mattered. More effort and better knowledge do not always increase together.

Donald Henderson, one of the programme’s leaders, recalled in 1980 that the 1967 manual had already made surveillance central: collecting and interpreting information, acting on it and circulating the findings. Surveillance was not a late invention added after nobody had thought to look. The harder task was making an existing commitment shape daily work.[2]

An organization can have the right sentence in its manual and still devote too little attention to it. People may accept that investigation matters while remaining occupied with a familiar activity that leaves no time to investigate. A procedure’s presence on paper and its capacity to correct practice are different accomplishments.

Henderson described experience in eastern Nigeria showing that reporting and intensive, targeted containment vaccination could interrupt transmission without very high population-wide immunity. Related experience followed elsewhere. This opened a practical possibility: find where transmission continued and concentrate action there, rather than assume that a larger aggregate total would answer every difficulty.[2]

It was not a discovery that vaccination was useless. Effective vaccine remained a crucial tool. The change concerned how evidence directed its use: locating cases, tracing contacts and organizing a prompt response. Investigation and action were connected, not rival alternatives. The purpose stayed recognizable while the way of pursuing it became more attentive to place.

Nor did one instruction instantly replace established practice. Henderson acknowledged how firmly many national leaders and advisers trusted mass vaccination, and how difficult it was to give surveillance sufficient attention. Seeing the significance of an approach did not automatically reorganize people’s time. An insight could arrive before the institution knew how to make room for it.[2]

Sanjoy Bhattacharya’s archival history of India adds another correction to the picture. WHO headquarters, regional staff, central government and local authorities negotiated and disagreed; resources and political support had to be secured repeatedly. A story in which international experts simply supplied the answer would remove much of the work through which an answer became usable.[3]

The programme’s capacity therefore existed in connections as well as offices. Someone local had to recognize a possible case; information had to travel; someone had to be able to respond. A global aim could not substitute for those links. It could help build them, but not dispense with the people whose knowledge made them work.
## The last case was not yet known to be the last

We now call the 1977 case the last naturally occurring one. At the time, that description still depended on what would be found afterwards. Naming a final case does not demonstrate that no later case has been missed. Certification had to address precisely the uncertainty that a confident retrospective sentence can conceal.

The certification approach joined elapsed time to detection capacity: at least two years after the last case, with surveillance adequate to detect disease. Two calendar years were not an automatic certificate. If the reason for not finding cases remained unclear, the passage of time alone could not turn the zero into reliable evidence.[1]

There is an ordinary version of this problem. If someone says an object is not in a room, we ask where they looked, whether the light was on and whether they checked the cupboard. We do not mean that nobody may ever reach a conclusion. We want to know what this failure to see warrants us in believing.

The rumour register served that kind of distinction. Reports could turn out to concern another disease or an old infection. Two confirmed smallpox cases recorded in the account came from the 1978 laboratory-associated outbreak in Birmingham. Last naturally occurring case must not quietly become no smallpox case of any kind afterwards.[1]

Investigating a report that turns out not to be smallpox is not necessarily wasted work. The report has neither been suppressed to protect an achievement nor treated as sufficient by itself to destroy the conclusion. Receiving information, examining it and deciding what it establishes are separate acts. A good route in still needs a responsible process afterwards.

That process requires judgment. A system counting every suspicion as a permanent confirmation could never finish. One accepting only information compatible with zero would have no reason to trust its own result. The useful space lies between them: accessible reporting, appropriate investigation and an explanation of what was found. Openness does not mean abandoning standards of evidence.

International certification was consequently more than a larger stamp placed on national announcements. Documentary review and field assessment had to support the result; the Global Commission brought the evidence together. The report’s foreword records the World Health Assembly’s acceptance of the eradication conclusions on 8 May 1980.[1]

The conclusion carried authority, but rank was not its only reason for being credible. Before it stood work that others could question: why were cases not being found, how had missed transmission been considered, and could evidence from different places be examined? Confidence became something more substantial than either politeness between governments or suspicion without an end.

This was a concrete capacity created through cooperation. People did not have to rely solely on another country saying that its problem was over. Nor did their inability to search the whole world personally require them to believe nothing. Jointly organized investigation and certification supplied grounds on which they could trust a conclusion they could not establish alone.

Yet learning how to act more effectively did not reduce every difficulty to a technical question. Once teams could find a person at risk of infection or transmission, another question remained: how could they treat that person in pursuit of the shared goal? Better information could make the question more immediate, not remove it.
## An achievement is not an answer about every method

Paul Greenough’s historical study examined episodes of intimidation and coercion during the South Asian campaign of 1973–1975, and the resistance they provoked. Such records need attention. They cannot be extended to every region or worker, and selected episodes cannot establish how frequently those practices occurred across the global programme.[4]

We need not choose between treating eradication as permission for everything and treating abuse as proof that nothing worthwhile occurred. Disease disappeared; that does not make every intervention acceptable. Objectionable conduct occurred; that does not erase the lives protected by vaccine, surveillance and coordinated work. These are different questions, not opposite totals to be cancelled against each other.

People exposed to transmission and people subjected to an intervention can both have reasons that deserve more than a slogan. Refusal does not make a contagious risk fall only on the person refusing. Protecting others does not remove the responsibility to explain the grounds, scope and manner of an intervention. The difficulty is that neither side can simply be deleted.

A state’s participation in an international programme was not an individual’s agreement to a particular encounter. We cannot insert that agreement on the person’s behalf because the international purpose was valuable. Nor can local hesitation automatically be explained as ignorance. Assessing a conflict requires knowing what happened there, not assigning positions from the programme’s final result.

This is not a demand to balance every success story with a matching list of faults. It is a demand to keep the questions distinguishable: whether disease was eradicated, how that was known, who made the work possible and whether someone experienced treatment that should not be overlooked. None of these answers can do all the others’ work.

The post-eradication arrangements did not abandon investigation and precautions altogether. WHO’s later account describes the 1980 policies as retaining suspected-case investigation, attention to laboratory stocks and necessary expertise. Success changed what work remained appropriate. It did not make every precaution pointless or every new report irrelevant.[6]

Conversely, keeping investigation possible does not mean forbidding the recognition of an achievement forever. Evidence should enable decisions, not supply an endlessly renewable reason to postpone them. The aim is a grounded conclusion that does not declare future relevant information inadmissible in advance. Neither certainty without examination nor examination without any possibility of concluding will serve.

This history stops with the 1980 certification and arrangements for what followed. It is not a recommendation to transplant historical interventions into present practice, or a claim that every disease fits the same approach. It concerns how people, without advance knowledge of the outcome, built reasons strong enough to guide action and eventually justify a conclusion.

Return to the register. Its value is not just that the entries did not overturn eradication. It is that a programme nearing success kept a route open for someone who might interrupt it. A serious statement that we have done it need not depend on making sure no further question can be heard.

sources.note_en: Primary WHO report, not a study authored by the hosting university. Official IRIS downloads returned an access page; relevant parts of the 122-page published report were read through this mirror: chapter 9, sections 11.1–11.5, Annex 12 and foreword. Detection and absence, certification and elapsed time, directly reported rumours and all local reports, and natural transmission and the Birmingham laboratory outbreak remain distinct. The prose/table discrepancy about 'more than half' being chickenpox or measles is not repeated; no ratio is used. Official catalogue: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/report-of-the-global-commission-for-the-certification-of-smallpox-eradication-wha33.3 .
sources.note_zh: WHO原始报告，不是托管大学撰写的研究。官方IRIS下载返回访问页面，改由此镜像核对122页出版版的相关部分：第九章、第11.1—11.5节、附件十二及序言。区分未发现与不存在、认证与时间、直接报WHO与全部地方传闻、自然传播与伯明翰实验室相关病例。不沿用正文与表格对水痘/麻疹占比的差异，不报该比例。官方目录：https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/report-of-the-global-commission-for-the-certification-of-smallpox-eradication-wha33.3 。

sources.note_en: First-person retrospective account hosted by CDC; especially pp.425–426 on the 1967 manual, eastern Nigeria and the difficulty of changing emphasis. It is a participant's account, not an independent verdict on all programme methods. Surveillance was already part of the intensified programme; vaccination did not cease when targeted containment gained emphasis. His period-specific views about other diseases are not adopted as current guidance.

sources.note_zh: 1995年原始历史研究，DOI 10.1016/0277-9536(95)00035-6。核对可访问摘要，仅据以说明研究涉及若干强制及抵触事件；原全文档案链接已跳至其他页面。不从摘要还原个别场景、不估计全球发生率，也不声称所有干预或成果均依靠强制。

sources.note_en: Used for intensified programme start in 1967, last known natural case in Somalia in 1977 and eradication declaration in 1980. Natural case is not every case of any origin; current programme descriptions are not projected backwards into the 1970s.
sources.note_zh: 核对1967年强化计划、1977年索马里最后已知自然病例及1980年宣告；自然病例不等于任何来源的一切病例，不把网页现时工作描述倒置到1970年代。

sources.title_en: WHO: Post-eradication, retrospective account dated 28 June 2016
sources.note_en: Used only as a retrospective explanation of the 1980 post-eradication policies, including investigation, stock management and retained expertise. No medical recommendation, current vaccine policy or assertion that eradication removed all future risks is inferred.
sources.note_zh: 仅用于回顾说明1980年后续政策的疑似病例调查、库存管理及能力保留；不据此给医疗建议、现行疫苗政策，也不把根除说成消除一切未来风险。
